## Study objective

The study tests whether pair formation is followed by convergence in sequence organization, individual phee-call acoustics, or both, and whether any change depends on the audience to which calls are directed.

## Study design

Three male and three female common marmosets were recorded in all nine possible male–female combinations. After three permanent pairs were formed and co-housed, the recording design was repeated four months later. Calls were therefore compared before and after pair formation and separately for partner and non-partner audiences.

## Acoustic and sequence representations

Sequence similarity was quantified using transition probabilities, bigram distributions, repeat-length distributions, and local sequence alignment. Individual phee-call similarity was quantified using spectro-temporal measurements, MFCC representations, constrained dynamic time warping, and a variational autoencoder.

The use of multiple representations at both levels tests whether the estimated pattern is robust to a particular feature set or distance metric.

## Results reported in the preprint

Following pair formation, partners showed increased sequence similarity when calling to non-partners. The combined model and three of four sequence measures supported this pattern; repeat-length distributions showed no clear change in the non-partner condition. No comparable convergence was detected in partner-directed sequences. Individual phee-call acoustics showed no clear convergence in either audience context across the four representations.

The estimated sequence-level change was therefore audience dependent rather than a general increase in similarity between partners. This pattern supports socially contingent plasticity in sequence production while leaving the underlying mechanism unresolved.

One interpretation is that sequence organization forms a pair-associated signature expressed toward non-partners. The production data support sequence-level flexibility, but do not establish receiver recognition, shared meaning, or a learned convention.

## Interpretation

Studies of vocal accommodation often emphasize the acoustic form of individual calls. These results show that sequence order and repetition can vary independently of individual-call acoustics and that audience context is necessary for interpreting convergence estimates.

## Limitations and planned tests

The study includes three pairs, and one pair lacked partner-after observations. The four-month interval between recording periods was not accompanied by an unpaired control group or repeated pre-pairing baseline; temporal drift, arousal, and other pair-specific changes therefore cannot be excluded. Playback or interactive experiments are required to test receiver perception and whether the convergent sequence features communicate pair affiliation.
